notes.9:4: The Vulgate reads "et inde ne exeatis" ("and do not go out from there"), instructing the apostles to stay in the same house rather than move about, whereas the Greek text reads positively ("and depart from there").
notes.9:10: The Clementine Vulgate reads "in locum desertum, qui est Bethsaidæ" ("into a deserted place that belongs to Bethsaida"), whereas critical Greek editions read "to a city called Bethsaida."
notes.9:26: Here and in 9:31 the Vulgate renders Greek "doxa" ("glory") as "majestas" ("majesty").
notes.9:35: The Vulgate reads "Filius meus dilectus" ("My beloved Son"), whereas critical Greek editions read "My Chosen One."
notes.9:43: In the Clementine Vulgate this verse combines what modern numbering divides into verses 43 and 44; it also reads "in cordibus vestris" ("in your hearts"), whereas the Greek text reads "into your ears."
notes.9:55: Here and in 9:56 the Clementine Vulgate includes Jesus's words ("You do not know what spirit you are of. The Son of Man did not come to destroy lives, but to save them."), which are omitted in critical Greek editions.
notes.10:11: The Clementine Vulgate reads simply 'that clung to us' (qui adhaesit nobis), without the phrase 'to our feet' found in Greek manuscripts.
notes.10:15: Where critical Greek editions read a question ('will you be exalted to heaven?'), the Vulgate has the participle exaltata ('exalted up to heaven'), followed by 'plunged down to the underworld' (usque ad infernum demergeris).
notes.10:27: Where Greek manuscripts use the singular 'strength,' the Vulgate renders the term in the plural as 'with all your powers' (ex omnibus virtutibus tuis).
notes.10:31: Both here (praeterivit) and in 10:32 (pertransiit), the Vulgate states simply that the priest and the Levite 'passed by' without adding 'on the other side.'
notes.10:42: The Vulgate uses the superlative 'the best part' (optimam partem), whereas the Greek text has the positive adjective 'the good part.'
notes.11:3: The Clementine Vulgate reads hodie ("today"), matching Matthew 6:11, whereas the Greek text of Luke reads "each day" or "day by day."
notes.11:8: The opening conditional clause "And if he persists in knocking" (Et si ille perseveraverit pulsans) is a distinctive Vulgate reading absent from the standard Greek text.
notes.11:13: The Clementine Vulgate reads spiritum bonum ("the good Spirit," or "a good spirit"), paralleling "good gifts," whereas the standard Greek text reads "the Holy Spirit."
notes.11:15: The Vulgate retains the Latin and Old Testament spelling Beelzebub here and in 11:18-19, whereas critical Greek editions read Beelzebul.
notes.11:41: Latin quod superest literally means "what remains over" or "your surplus," whereas the Greek text (ta enonta) means "the things that are inside."
notes.11:53: The Clementine Vulgate begins with "while He was saying these things to them" (vs. critical Greek "when He went out from there"), names "the Pharisees and the experts in the law" (vs. Greek "scribes and Pharisees"), and renders Greek apostomatizein ("question closely") literally as os ejus opprimere ("press upon His mouth").
notes.12:1: Vulgate reads multis turbis circumstantibus ("many crowds standing around") and omits "first" before "to His disciples," where the Greek text has "myriads of the crowd gathered together" and "to His disciples first."
notes.12:3: Vulgate reads Quoniam ... dicentur ("For ... will be said"), whereas the Greek text reads "Therefore ... will be heard."
notes.12:6: Latin dipondio (dupondius) is a Roman bronze coin worth two asses, rendering the Greek "two assaria."
notes.12:25: Vulgate reads cogitando ("by thinking," distinct from solliciti in 12:22 and 12:26) and staturam ("stature," physical height), whereas the Greek wording is often taken as "by worrying" and "lifespan."
notes.12:29: Vulgate reads nolite in sublime tolli ("do not be lifted up on high"), rendering the Greek verb for anxious suspense literally by its spatial image of being lifted aloft, which Latin commentators also understood as a warning against pride or ambitious restlessness.
notes.12:31: Vulgate reads quærite primum regnum Dei, et justitiam ejus ("seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness") and hæc omnia ("all these things"), echoing Matthew 6:33, whereas the critical Greek text reads simply "seek His kingdom, and these things."
notes.12:35: Vulgate includes in manibus vestris ("in your hands"), a phrase not present in the standard Greek text.
notes.12:46: Latin dividet eum literally means "will divide him" (here "will sever him"), translating the Greek verb meaning "cut in two" while also linking to "his portion" (partem ejus).
notes.12:49: Vulgate reads et quid volo nisi ut accendatur? ("and what do I want except that it be kindled?"), whereas the Greek can be read as an exclamation, "and how I wish it were already kindled!"
notes.12:56: Vulgate places "the sky and the earth" (cæli et terræ) in that order, whereas the Greek has "the earth and the sky."
notes.13:3: The Vulgate shifts from poenitentiam habueritis ("have repentance") here to poenitentiam non egeritis ("do not repent," literally "do not do repentance") in verse 5, varying its rendering of the Greek verb for repenting.
notes.13:9: The Latin preserves an abrupt break in syntax (aposiopesis) after "if indeed it bears fruit" without supplying an implied "well," and places in futurum ("in the future") clearly with the second clause ("you will cut it down").
notes.13:10: The Vulgate reads in synagoga eorum ("in their synagogue"), whereas the Greek text reads "in one of the synagogues."
notes.13:25: The Vulgate reads intraverit ("has entered") rather than the Greek "has risen up."
notes.13:31: The Vulgate reads In ipsa die ("On that very day"), whereas the Greek text reads "In that very hour."
notes.14:5: The Vulgate reads asinus, aut bos ("a donkey or an ox"), whereas critical Greek editions generally read "a son or an ox."
notes.14:10: The Vulgate omits "all" before "those reclining together," whereas most Greek manuscripts read "all who sit at table with you."
notes.14:24: The Vulgate reads Dico autem vobis ("And I tell you") where the Greek has "For I tell you."
notes.14:28: The Vulgate expands the Greek "the cost" into sumptus, qui necessarii sunt ("the expenses that are necessary").
notes.15:1: The Clementine Vulgate lacks "all" (Greek pantes) before "tax collectors and sinners."
notes.15:7: Latin ita ... quam preserves an elliptical comparative without an explicit "more." Poenitentiam agente (literally "doing repentance," also in 15:10 and 16:30) is the Vulgate idiom for repentance and is rendered "repents" in keeping with the other Gospel occurrences.
notes.15:10: The Vulgate uses the future tense "erit" ("there will be joy," matching 15:7) rather than the Greek present tense ("there is joy").
notes.15:30: The Vulgate reads "substantiam suam" ("his property," referring to the younger son's divided share), whereas Greek manuscripts read "your livelihood/property."
notes.16:6: Latin "cados" ("jars," rendering the Hebrew liquid measure bath, roughly eight to nine gallons) and "coros" in 16:7 ("cors," a dry measure of roughly ten to twelve bushels) represent substantial commercial debts.
notes.16:9: The Vulgate reads the second-person plural "cum defeceritis" ("when you fail," meaning when your life comes to an end), whereas modern critical Greek editions read third-person singular ("when it [wealth] fails"). Latin "mammona" (also in 16:11, 13) transliterates the Aramaic term for worldly wealth.
notes.16:21: The clause "et nemo illi dabat" ("and no one gave him any") is a distinctive Vulgate reading echoing 15:16 and is absent from most Greek manuscripts.
notes.16:22: The Clementine Vulgate attaches "in inferno" ("in the underworld," rendering Greek hades) to "was buried" at the end of verse 22, whereas the Greek text places it at the beginning of verse 23.
notes.16:25: Latin "hic" can be read either as the pronoun "he/this man" (contrasting directly with "tu," "you") or as the adverb "here" (matching Greek hode); in 16:31, Vulgate "credent" ("will they believe") differs from Greek "will they be persuaded."
notes.17:6: The Clementine Vulgate uses future indicatives (habueritis ... dicetis ... obediet, 'If you have ... you will say ... it will obey'), casting the saying as a future condition rather than the contrary-to-fact conditional ('would say ... would obey') of the Greek text.
notes.17:10: The Clementine Vulgate begins verse 10 with non puto ('I do not think so'), a phrase omitted in most modern critical Greek texts and placed at the end of verse 9 in the Textus Receptus.
notes.17:21: Latin intra vos explicitly renders the debated Greek expression entos hymon as 'within you' rather than 'among you' or 'in your midst'.
notes.17:31: Latin In illa hora ('In that hour') is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Greek text has 'on that day'.
notes.17:35: The Latin text includes the clause 'two in the field: one will be taken up, and the other will be left behind' at the end of verse 35; it is traditionally numbered as verse 36, and the line is omitted in most modern critical Greek texts.
notes.18:5: Latin sugillet literally means "bruise" or "beat black and blue," and figuratively "harass" or "wear down."
notes.18:7: The Vulgate has the future tense "and will He have patience with them?" (et patientiam habebit in illis?), which can refer either to God's forbearance toward His chosen ones or to His apparent delay in their case.
notes.18:8: The Vulgate includes the parenthetical verb putas ("do you think"), rendering the Greek emphatic interrogative particle explicitly.
notes.18:20: The Clementine Vulgate places "you shall not kill" (non occides) before "you shall not commit adultery" (non moechaberis) and uses future indicatives, whereas the Greek text of Luke reverses those two commandments.
notes.18:32: The Clementine Vulgate reads flagellabitur ("flogged") where the Greek text has "mistreated" or "insulted," anticipating the repeated verb flagellaverint in verse 33.
notes.19:26: The Clementine Vulgate adds et abundabit ('and he will have an abundance') and the final ab eo ('from him'), whereas standard Greek editions of Luke omit both phrases.
notes.19:30: The Vulgate specifies pullum asinae ('a donkey's colt', literally 'the colt of a female donkey'), while the Greek text reads simply 'a colt.'
notes.19:31: The Vulgate renders the response with operam ejus desiderat ('desires its service') here but uses eum necessarium habet ('needs it') in verse 34, whereas the Greek uses the same phrase in both verses.
notes.19:32: The Vulgate explicitly adds stantem pullum ('the colt standing'), which is not present in the Greek text.
notes.19:47: The Clementine Vulgate reads the singular princeps plebis ('the leader of the people'), whereas the Greek text has the plural ('the leading men of the people').
notes.20:23: The Clementine Vulgate includes "Why do you test Me?" (Quid me tentatis?), a clause absent from several early Greek manuscripts of Luke 20:23 though present in Matthew 22:18 and Mark 12:15.
notes.20:30: The Vulgate reads "And the next took her, and he also died without a son" (Et sequens accepit illam, et ipse mortuus est sine filio), using "the next" (sequens) rather than "the second" and preserving the longer clause with singular "without a son," which several early Greek manuscripts omit.
notes.20:35: Where the Greek repeats "neither marry nor are given in marriage," the Vulgate uses Roman marital idiom, "will neither marry nor take wives" (neque nubent, neque ducent uxores).
notes.20:36: The Clementine Vulgate prints the perfect-tense form potuerunt ("could"), whereas the Greek has the present "are able" and critical Vulgate editions read the future poterunt ("will be able").
notes.20:37: The Vulgate renders the Greek phrase meaning "in the passage about the bush" literally as a spatial preposition, "beside the bush" (secus rubum).
notes.21:19: Latin possidebitis animas vestras uses the future indicative of possideo ("you will possess your souls"), contrasting with Greek traditions that read an imperative or emphasize gaining one's life.
notes.21:20: Latin ab exercitu is singular ("by an army"), whereas the Greek text uses the plural ("armies" or "encampments").
notes.21:26: Latin arescentibus hominibus literally means "with people withering away" (drying up), a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Greek participle meaning "fainting" or "expiring."
notes.21:30: The Vulgate (cum producunt jam ex se fructum, scitis) explicitly includes "fruit" (fructum), connects ex se ("from themselves") to the trees rather than the observers, and omits the Greek participle "seeing."
notes.21:36: Latin ut digni habeamini ("so that you may be deemed worthy") follows the textual reading preserved in the Vulgate and Majority Greek tradition, whereas several older Greek manuscripts read "so that you may have strength."
notes.22:20: Vulgate reads future passive "fundetur" ("will be poured out") and third-person singular "postquam coenavit" ("after He had dined"), where critical Greek texts have a present participle ("being poured out") and an infinitive ("after supper"). The Latin masculine relative "qui" ("which") can refer to either "calix" ("cup") or "sanguine" ("blood").
notes.22:26: Vulgate pairs "major" ("greater/greatest") directly with "minor" ("lesser/least," which can also mean "younger"), corresponding to the Greek "neoteros" ("younger").
notes.22:31: Vulgate explicitly introduces a new speech with "Ait autem Dominus" ("And the Lord said"), which is omitted in critical Greek editions. Here "vos" ("you") is plural, shifting to singular "te" and "tu" ("you") addressed to Peter alone in verse 32.
notes.22:36: Vulgate leaves the object of "qui non habet" ("the one who has none") unexpressed and reads "tunicam" ("tunic") rather than "cloak." Jesus's speech continues directly into verse 37.
notes.22:43: Vulgate includes verses 43-44 in full, places "Et factus in agonia, prolixius orabat" in verse 43 rather than verse 44, and uses "prolixius" ("at greater length") where the Greek has "ektenesteron" ("more earnestly").
notes.22:51: Latin "Sinite usque huc" ("Allow it this far") is concise and can be understood either as telling the disciples to stop resisting or as asking the arresting party to permit Him to heal the wounded servant.
notes.22:68: Vulgate includes both "mihi" ("Me") and "neque dimittetis" ("nor will you release Me"), which are omitted in many critical Greek editions. Likewise, Vulgate places the council's question ("If You are the Christ, tell us") at the end of verse 66 rather than the beginning of verse 67.
notes.23:11: The Vulgate renders the Greek for "splendid/bright garment" specifically as veste alba ("a white garment").
notes.23:15: The Clementine Vulgate reads nam remisi vos ad illum ("for I sent you to him"), contrasting with critical Greek texts that read "for he sent him back to us"; ei ("by Him") functions as a dative of agent with actum est.
notes.23:33: Latin Calvariae is the genitive of calvaria ("skull") and the origin of the English name "Calvary"; here and in v. 39 the Vulgate shifts to latrones ("robbers"), whereas v. 32 uses nequam ("wicked men").
notes.23:42: The Clementine Vulgate retains the address Domine ("Lord") rather than "Jesus," and translates "into Your kingdom" (in regnum tuum, accusative) rather than "in Your kingdom."
notes.23:56: Latin siluerunt literally means "kept silent" or "kept still," reflecting the Vulgate's rendering of Sabbath stillness and cessation from work.
notes.24:17: In the Clementine Vulgate, 'et estis tristes?' ('and you are sad?') is part of Jesus's question, whereas modern critical Greek texts close the question after 'while walking' and add a narrative clause ('and they stood still, looking sad').
notes.24:36: The Clementine Vulgate includes 'ego sum, nolite timere' ('it is I, do not be afraid') after 'Peace to you,' a reading attested in several Greek and Old Latin witnesses but omitted in modern critical Greek editions.
notes.24:42: The Clementine Vulgate includes 'et favum mellis' ('and a honeycomb') alongside the roasted fish, whereas modern critical Greek editions omit this phrase.
notes.24:43: The Clementine Vulgate adds 'sumens reliquias dedit eis' ('taking what remained, He gave it to them'), a reading rooted in Latin tradition and a few Greek and Syriac witnesses but absent from most Greek manuscripts.
notes.24:53: The Clementine Vulgate includes both 'laudantes et benedicentes' ('praising and blessing') and the concluding 'Amen,' whereas modern critical Greek editions omit 'praising and' as well as 'Amen.'
